questions.question: How can I attach one more element after the last element of a list?

raw_answer.answer:
The list methods make it very easy to use a list as a stack, where the last element added is the first element retrieved (“last-in, first-out”). [1]

It is also possible to use a list as a queue, where the first element added is the first element retrieved (“first-in, first-out”); however, lists are not efficient for this purpose. [2]

For a positive step , the contents of a range r are determined by the formula r[i] = start + step*i where i >= 0 and r[i] < stop . [2]

The given end point is never part of the generated sequence; range(10) generates 10 values, the legal indices for items of a sequence of length 10. [3]

The range type represents an immutable sequence of numbers and is commonly used for looping a specific number of times in for loops. [4]

questions.question: What Python facility gives separate package environments to different applications?

raw_answer.answer:
The solution for this problem is to create a virtual environment , a self-contained directory tree that contains a Python installation for a particular version of Python, plus a number of additional packages. [1]

Python applications will often use packages and modules that don’t come as part of the standard library. [2]

In addition to the standard library, there is an active collection of hundreds of thousands of components (from individual programs and modules to packages and entire application development frameworks), available from the Python Package Index . [3]

For Unix-like operating systems Python is normally provided as a collection of packages, so it may be necessary to use the packaging tools provided with the operating system to obtain some or all of the optional components. [4]

questions.question: How do list comprehensions create lists, and how does range choose its stopping point?

raw_answer.answer:
A list comprehension consists of brackets containing an expression followed by a for clause, then zero or more for or if clauses. [1]

>>> range(10) range(0, 10) In many ways the object returned by range() behaves as if it is a list, but in fact it isn’t. [2]

The advantage of the range type over a regular list or tuple is that a range object will always take the same (small) amount of memory, no matter the size of the range it represents (as it only stores the start , stop and step values, calculating individual items and subranges as needed). [3]
